newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poll shows most Germans support coal deal.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows most Germans support coal deal.

text.p: An opinion poll showed on Friday that almost three quarters of Germans approved of a deal struck by Chancellor Helmut Kohl with miners'leaders over planned subsidy cuts.

The Forsa Institute polling unit said most Germans supported a slow decline in coal subsidies, along the lines of a deal struck by Kohl with the mining union on Thursday to avoid mass layoffs while slashing coal subsidies.

The agreement convinced thousands of miners to end protests which had blocked the Bonn government district for three days. The institute said 72 percent of those polled thought the miners' protest was justified.

Bonn pledged to pump 900 million marks ($530 million) more than planned into the dying industry by the year 2000, but stuck to its plan to cut the annual level of federal subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) in 2005 from nine billion now.
Forsa said 16 percent of those polled were against all subsidies and five percent supported drastic cuts, even if that meant the loss of many jobs in the sector.
But some German newspapers said the government had paid a high price for peace with its miners over subsidy cuts and had set a dangerous precedent by giving into their demands.

"The demonstrating miners came to Bonn to claim "their' money and they largely acheived their goal," the daily Die Welt said in an editorial. "The danger is great that the case will set a bad precedent."
Die Welt said every economic interest group would now think it could achieve its goal by putting pressure on politicians.

The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung attacked both the coal deal and a 25 billion mark ($14.57 billion) investment drive unveiled by Kohl on Wednesday, saying they represented naive and old-fashioned interventionist policies.
"The idea that the economic crisis, manifest in unemployment figures, can be kept under control by government cash, could soon turn out to be an illusion," it wrote.

But the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung said the coal deal meant Germany, which looked like it was teetering on the edge of dangerous confrontation between workers and employers, was still committed to a compromise style of politics.
The paper said the agreement set a good example for those engaged in talks over the government's planned tax reform.

The Bonn daily Gerneral Anzeiger said nobody could be completely satisfied with the agreement, but said at least it had cleared the way for necessary reform talks between the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and the government.
The SPD pulled out of tax talks after the government announced its subsidy cut plans and said they would only return to negotiations if a satisfactory compromise was reached.
"There is still time before Easter to get the urgently necessary reforms on their way," the General Anzeiger said.
